title: A Blind Man Sees, Leaders Don't
overview: Jesus heals a man born blind, and as religious leaders question and finally expel him, the story turns into a contrast between those who come to see and those who refuse to.

parts.label: Whose fault is it? (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Many people then assumed that serious suffering was punishment for someone's sin, so the disciples ask who is to blame. Jesus rejects that link and treats the man's condition as a moment for God's work to show, calling himself the light of the world and setting up the chapter's theme of seeing.

parts.label: Mud and the pool (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: Saliva was a common folk remedy at the time, and Jesus sends the man to wash in Siloam, a well-known pool in Jerusalem. The writer notes that Siloam means "Sent," likely a hint at Jesus, whom this Gospel often calls the one sent by God.

parts.label: A Sabbath dispute (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: The Sabbath was the weekly day of rest, and by the leaders' rules, making mud and healing a condition that wasn't urgent counted as forbidden work. So the Pharisees, a group devoted to careful keeping of the law, split between "he breaks the rules, so he isn't from God" and "how could a sinner do this?"

parts.label: Frightened parents (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: Being put out of the synagogue meant being cut off from the local community's worship and much of its social life, so the parents carefully avoid saying anything about Jesus. Many scholars think this detail also reflects the experience of Jesus' followers decades later, when the Gospel was written and they were separating from synagogues.

parts.label: The man stands firm (vv. 24-34)
parts.note: "Give glory to God" was a formal demand to tell the truth, almost like taking an oath, but the man sticks to the one thing he knows and turns their own reasoning against them. Unable to answer him, they insult him as "born in sin," still tying his blindness to guilt, and throw him out.

parts.label: Who is really blind? (vv. 35-41)
parts.note: Jesus seeks out the man who was thrown out, and he comes to believe and worships him (early copies differ on whether Jesus says "Son of Man" or "Son of God"). Jesus then uses sight as a picture: as it is usually read, those who admit they cannot see can be given sight, while those certain they already see stay where they are.

disagreement: Christians differ over verse 3: some read it as saying God allowed or even intended the man's blindness so that God's work could be shown, while others read it only as Jesus rejecting blame and saying God can act within suffering, without explaining why the suffering happened.
think: When have you been most sure you saw a situation clearly, and what might have been hard to admit you were missing?
